chapter_theme: Folly (பேதைமை): the fool enjoys a world in which death is already at work, puts off virtue, relies on birth and status, clings to the rich and the unworthy, praises himself and quarrels for nothing. Most quatrains are comparisons that make his position look absurd.
structure_note: 331 and 332 are paired similes of misjudged time: the turtle in the heating pot and the bathers waiting for the sea to fall silent. 333 and 334 set status against usefulness. 335 to 340 show the fool among others: angry, ingratiating, clinging, rejecting, boastful.

331.reading: As a turtle put in a pot by its killers, with the fire lit beneath, plays in the water without knowing its state, so are those who revel in this world's net while Death, the great killer, waits for the moment to seize them.
331.nuance: The water the turtle enjoys is what will kill it, just as the world's pleasures are the net. Mudaliar notes that மாண்பு ('worth') is used ironically.

332.reading: Those who say they will see to virtue once the household's unfinished tasks are done are like people who went to bathe in the great sea and said they would bathe when its roar had died down.
332.nuance: Household duties, like the noise of the sea, never stop, so the simile turns postponement into permanent refusal.

333.reading: Though one has all five, high caste, austerity, learning, standing and age, without lack, not knowing the good, stainless and anciently honoured உலகம் makes it all like milk-rice without ghee.
333.nuance: The commentators also divide on குடி: household prosperity for Mudaliar, good family for Shanmuganar. Pope's 'thin, watery milk' departs from the Tamil, which has rice without ghee.

positions.position: உலகம் means the worlds to be reached after this life, heaven and release, so what the fool lacks is knowledge of what leads there.
உலகம் means the ways of the world, and what the fool lacks is knowledge of how to live by them.

334.reading: Stones are far better than base people: though they cannot understand words either, they serve whoever comes to them, at once, for standing, sitting, lying and walking on.
334.nuance: The comparison is not about intelligence, which both lack, but about use: the stone at least gives itself to others.

335.reading: Though nothing is gained by it, the fool, as if he had gained something, grows angry even with those who don't deserve it, and if he cannot string harsh words together and say them, a fierce itch gnaws at his tongue.
335.nuance: The targets are read three ways: Mudaliar's ஏலாதார் are those for whom such anger is unfitting, Shanmuganar's (printed under 334) are superiors who are no match for the fool, and Pope's are those who will not or cannot contend with him.

336.reading: Those who follow people without good conduct, saying 'we will make them bow to us', have a poor kind of friendship, lord of the shore where the laurel with fine shoots flowers: it is like losing one's hand pinching a rock.
336.nuance: Mudaliar calls the bond a one-sided friendship and cites a Pazhamozhi line saying no one pinches a rock and keeps their hand. Pope supplies 'wealthy' for the people followed.

337.reading: If there is ghee inside a pot, ants keep circling its outside without leaving, though they cannot get at it; so people cling to the wealthy and won't leave them, though they give nothing.
337.nuance: The quatrain describes a habit of the world without blaming it in so many words; being placed in this chapter is what marks the habit as folly.

338.reading: They gain no good thing day by day, do no virtue, give nothing to the needy, never hold their beloved in their arms, and do not live with renown: will they not come to loathe the days they live?
338.nuance: The list mixes virtue, giving, married love and fame, so the fool fails at every aim of life, not only at renunciation. Mudaliar allows நல்லவை to be read as நல் அவை, a good assembly, and Shanmuganar takes that reading.

339.reading: When one person admires and seeks another who answers 'we don't want you', that friendship with those lacking discerning goodness is painful, even if it should yield the whole earth girdled by the roaring sea.
339.nuance: Mudaliar calls the bond a one-sided friendship, or a false one. The fool is the one who rejects the regard offered, but the warning is for the one who keeps offering it.

340.reading: Learning, wide gentleness and good birth win honour when others praise them; if a man praises them himself, his brothers-in-law multiply and mock him as a madman no medicine can cure.
340.nuance: Mudaliar explains மைத்துனர் (brothers-in-law) as mockers: the joking relationship stands for ridicule.

links.note: 337 mocks those who cannot know they will live another moment yet plan in crores; 331's turtle is a picture of that ignorance.
36 says to do virtue without saying 'we'll see to it then' (அன்றறிவாம்); 332 mocks the household version of the same words (மற்றறிவாம்).

On Shanmuganar's reading the two make the same claim: learning without knowing how to live with the world is still ignorance. On Mudaliar's reading, where உலகம் is the worlds after death, the link does not hold.
Both compare a person without human quality to an inert thing, a tree in 997 and a stone in 334. 334 goes further and ranks the stone above the person for its usefulness.
Both put the fool's urge to speak in an itching tongue (சுனை): in 313 the itch to debate, here the itch to abuse.
Both warn against following those who do not accept you. 967 counts the cost in honour; 336 in futility.
304 says the worthy will not stand behind the hoarding rich; 337 says people at large do. 304 describes the exception to 337's rule.
Both list the goods a fool's life lacks: 327 enjoyment, giving and the good path; 338 adds love and renown.
816 rates being a stranger to the wise far above close friendship with a fool; 339 says friendship with the undiscerning is painful even if it brought the whole earth.
978 says smallness adorns itself in self-admiration; 340 shows the self-praiser mocked as mad.

source_issues: Quatrain 333: the Tamil reads குடிநம்முப் பைந்தும், apparently for குடிமூப் பைந்தும்; Mudaliar glosses குடிமை and மூப்பு, and all three readings count five things including age.

Quatrain 334: Shanmuganar's field also holds the text of quatrain 335 with his commentary on it, and then the text of quatrain 336. Quatrains 335 and 336 have no Shanmuganar commentary aligned, and none on 336 appears anywhere. Mudaliar's gloss on 334 reads நளி for the verse's நனி.
Quatrain 338: Shanmuganar's field begins with the quatrain's last line before the commentary.
Quatrain 340: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of chapter 35.
